title: Shortest Palindrome
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every candidate prefix directly versus a KMP prefix-suffix array on a combined string.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a string s, find the shortest possible palindrome that can be formed by adding characters only in front of s (the original s must remain untouched at the end).

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s, find the shortest possible palindrome that can be formed by adding characters only in front of s (the original s must remain untouched at the end).

blocks.title: Analogy: Mirroring Just Enough of the Ending Onto the Front
blocks.text: Like looking at a word that almost mirrors itself and figuring out the fewest extra letters that need to be added at the very front so the whole thing reads identically forward and backward.

blocks.caption: Add the fewest possible characters, only at the front, to make the whole string a palindrome

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "aacecaaa"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The prefix \"aacecaa\" is already a palindrome","only the final \"a\" is left over","this 7 character prefix mirrors perfectly around its middle \"e\""],["Prepend the reverse of the leftover part (\"a\")","\"a\" + \"aacecaaa\"","reversing a single character leaves it unchanged"],["Answer","\"aaacecaaa\"","the shortest possible palindrome ending in the untouched original s"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "abcd"

blocks.text: Edge case: s is already a palindrome, like "aba"
Since s is already a palindrome, nothing needs to be added at all, so the answer is simply "aba", unchanged.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask exactly which prefix of s matters, and whether a familiar tool can identify it without checking every length separately.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The shortest palindrome is achieved by finding the longest prefix of s that is already a palindrome, then mirroring only the leftover suffix onto the front, since that leftover is exactly what still needs to be balanced.

Observation 2: The brute force checks every candidate prefix length independently, recomputing the palindrome comparison completely from scratch each time.

Observation 3: Longest Happy Prefix already showed the KMP prefix-suffix array's final value directly measures how much a string overlaps with itself in a single linear pass, but that technique compares a string against itself, not against a different, related string.

Observation 4: A prefix of s is a palindrome exactly when it equals its own reverse, which is the same as saying that prefix of s is also a suffix of reverse(s); building a combined string, s plus a separator plus reverse(s), and running the same LPS construction on it makes its final value directly measure the longest palindromic prefix of s, confirmed by tracing s equal to "aacecaaa" through to the correct combined LPS value, 7, and the correct final answer, "aaacecaaa".

Recognizing that a palindromic prefix of s is exactly a prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s) is what lets the familiar KMP prefix-suffix array answer this problem directly, once run on the right combined string.
6. Brute Force Solution
Find the longest prefix of s that is itself a palindrome by directly checking candidate prefixes from longest to shortest, then prepend the reverse of whatever is left over after that prefix.
Step by step algorithm

items: Starting from the full length of s and working downward, check whether the prefix of that length is a palindrome.
Take the first (longest) length that passes the check.
Reverse everything after that prefix and prepend it to the original string.

codes.python:
def shortest_palindrome(s):
    n = len(s)
    for length in range(n, 0, -1):
        prefix = s[:length]
        if prefix == prefix[::-1]:                                # direct palindrome check for this candidate
            suffix_to_add = s[length:][::-1]
            return suffix_to_add + s
    return s[::-1] + s if s else s


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "aacecaaa"
    print(shortest_palindrome(s))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Candidate lengths are tried from longest to shortest, so the very first palindrome found is guaranteed to be the longest possible one.
Whatever remains after the longest palindromic prefix is exactly the part that still needs to be mirrored to complete the palindrome.
Reversing that leftover and placing it at the very front, ahead of the unchanged original s, produces a valid palindrome using the fewest possible added characters.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Checking prefixes from longest to shortest correctly finds the longest palindromic prefix, and prepending the reversed leftover produces the shortest valid answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking up to n candidate prefixes, each costing up to O(n) to verify.
Space: O(n), for the substrings being built and compared.

Limitation: each candidate prefix length is checked completely independently, recomputing the palindrome comparison from scratch, when the same underlying self-matching structure can be computed once using the KMP prefix-suffix technique.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it verifies every candidate prefix length independently, recomputing an entire palindrome check from scratch at each one.

What the KMP prefix-suffix array fixes when applied to the right combined string: it captures self overlap information for an entire string in one linear pass, but needs to compare s against reverse(s), not against itself.

Why concatenating with a separator works: joining s, a character guaranteed not to appear in s, and reverse(s) lets the standard LPS construction measure exactly how much of s's prefix also appears as a suffix of reverse(s).

The core idea: build that combined string once, compute its prefix-suffix array once, and read the longest palindromic prefix length directly from its very last value.

Build a new string by concatenating s, a separator character that never appears in s, and the reverse of s. Then compute the standard KMP "longest proper prefix which is also a suffix" array for this combined string. The value at the very last position of that array gives exactly the length of the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of the reverse of s, which is precisely the longest palindromic prefix of s.
9. Optimized Solution
Build the combined string once, compute its prefix-suffix array, and read the answer's length directly from the last value.
Dry run for s = "aacecaaa"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Combined string","\"aacecaaa#aaacecaa\" (s + separator + reverse of s)"],["Prefix-suffix value at the last position","7"],["Longest palindromic prefix of s","s[0:7] = \"aacecaa\""],["Leftover to reverse and prepend","s[7:] = \"a\", reversed is still \"a\""],["Final answer","\"a\" + \"aacecaaa\" = \"aaacecaaa\""]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a combined string with a separator, its prefix-suffix array reveals the longest palindromic prefix

codes.python:
def shortest_palindrome(s):
    if not s:
        return s
    combined = s + '#' + s[::-1]
    n = len(combined)
    lps = [0] * n
    length = 0
    i = 1
    while i < n:
        if combined[i] == combined[length]:
            length += 1
            lps[i] = length
            i += 1
        elif length > 0:
            length = lps[length - 1]
        else:
            lps[i] = 0
            i += 1
    palindromic_prefix_length = lps[n - 1]
    suffix_to_add = s[palindromic_prefix_length:][::-1]
    return suffix_to_add + s


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "aacecaaa"
    print(shortest_palindrome(s))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the prefix-suffix array of the combined string tracks, at its very last position, how much of the entire first part (s) matches as a suffix ending at that position, and since the second part is reverse(s), that matched amount is exactly the length of the longest prefix of s that reads the same as a suffix of reverse(s), which is precisely a palindrome by definition.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The separator character is included between s and reverse(s)","It guarantees the two halves can never spuriously overlap across their boundary","The measured overlap is always a genuine match entirely within s and its reverse, never an accidental boundary crossing artifact"],["s is already a full palindrome","The prefix-suffix array's last value equals the full length of s","No characters need to be added at all, and the leftover to reverse and prepend is empty"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), building the combined string and its prefix-suffix array in one linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the combined string and its prefix-suffix array.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The separator character between s and its reverse is essential: without it, the prefix-suffix array could accidentally detect a spurious match that spans across the boundary between the two halves, so a character guaranteed not to appear in s (or a length marker) is required to keep the two halves cleanly separated.
Common Mistakes

items: Omitting the separator character, which can silently produce an incorrect, overly long palindromic prefix length.
Confusing which half of the combined string ends up giving the answer, forgetting that only s's own characters (not the reversed copy) form the final result.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Connect this problem explicitly to "Longest Happy Prefix" and general KMP preprocessing, since recognizing that the same prefix-suffix array technique solves both problems demonstrates a much deeper understanding than memorizing this problem in isolation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every prefix independently", think: build s plus a separator plus reverse(s), and read the answer from its prefix-suffix array.
If the interviewer says "why is the separator character necessary", think: without it, the array could detect a false match spanning across the boundary between s and its reverse.
If the interviewer says "how does this relate to Longest Happy Prefix", think: both problems read a specific answer directly off the same KMP prefix-suffix array construction, just applied to different combined strings.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does a prefix of s being a palindrome correspond exactly to it also being a suffix of reverse(s)?
Why is the separator character necessary, and what could go wrong without one?
How would you solve this if characters could only be added at the end of s instead of the front?
How would you find the shortest palindrome achievable by adding characters at both the front and the back?
How does this problem's technique relate to the one used in Longest Happy Prefix?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Longest Happy Prefix, whose KMP prefix-suffix array construction is reused here, applied to a combined string instead of the original string alone.
Repeated Substring Pattern, the first problem in this sheet to introduce the KMP prefix-suffix array, whose construction code is identical across all three of these problems.

Any problem asking about a relationship between a string and its own reverse, where concatenating the two with a separator and applying a standard string matching technique is a powerful, reusable trick.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space. Optimized (KMP prefix-suffix array on a combined string): O(n) time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: the KMP prefix-suffix array, computed on s concatenated with a separator and the reverse of s, to find the longest palindromic prefix directly.

Core Idea: a palindromic prefix of s is exactly a prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s), so running the familiar LPS construction on s plus a separator plus reverse(s) reads that length directly off the array's last value.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: a familiar self overlap technique can be redirected to compare a string against a different, related string, simply by concatenating them thoughtfully with a separator.
Interview Difficulty: the LPS construction itself is standard once known; recognizing to concatenate with reverse(s) and a separator is the specific creative leap this problem demands.
One line memory trick: build s plus separator plus reverse(s), the LPS array's last value is the longest palindromic prefix length.
